messages.subject: model definitions
parts:
Hi,=0D
=0D
I am a true beginner with Distance. I just started to study Distance 5.0 =
user=92s guide to get needed background and feedback to run analyses in D=
istance. I started to study Model Definitions, however I cannot find any =
more detailed information on use of the four basic types of Model Definit=
ions. There are four model definitions: half-normal/cosine, hazard/polyno=
mial, uniform/cosine and half-normal/hermite. I would like to know when t=
o apply which type of model definition and to what type of analysis. I wo=
uld like to know advantages and disadvantages of each model and its usage=
, when to use it, what types of data are designed individual models on, e=
tc. I could not find any of these more detailed informations in the progr=
am manual. Could you please simply explain me these issues in a practical=
way or e-mail me a recommended literature to read. I am rather intereste=
d in practically written materials than statistical publications since I =
am biologist not a statistician. I very app
reciate your time and effort.=0D
=0D
=0D
Best regards=0D
=0D
=0D
Martin=0D

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: model definitions
parts:
Hi Martin,

Below, I reproduce a page from Chapter 1 of the Users guide that answers
your general question about recommended literature. Your specific
questions about the different detection functions are answered in
chapters 1-3 of the introductory book. The book is written with
different users in mind, but chapters 1 and 2 are hopefully quite
accessable to biologists, as are the later chapters on line and point
transects, with their worked examples. Perhaps others can suggest
introductory (but necessarily less comprehensive) texts.

Good luck with your work,

- Len Thomas


------------------------------------------------------------------------
Distance Sampling Reference Books

The standard reference for conventional distance sampling methods is:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers,
D.L. and Thomas, L. 2001. Introduction to Distance Sampling. Oxford
University Press, London.

The book describes the methods in detail, as well as covering aspects of
survey design and giving several worked examples. It updates the
previous standard work:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P. and Laake, J.L. 1993.
Distance Sampling: Estimating Abundance of Biological Populations.
Chapman and Hall, London, reprinted 1999 by RUWPA, University of St.
Andrews, Scotland.

The 1993 book is still available for download over the internet at no
charge, at:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.book/

The advanced methods in this software are described in the following book:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers,
D.L. and Thomas, L. (editors) 2004. Advanced Distance Sampling. Oxford
University Press, London.

This book describes automated survey design methods, multiple covariate
distance sampling and mark-recapture distance sampling. In addition
methods are described that are not currently in Distance but which we
hope to include in the future, such as spatial modelling of density and
adaptive distance sampling.

--
